question: Can revealed-label Bayesian evidence reduce the cross-benchmark failure of a transferred prior?
candidate: Update component weights by the beta-binomial marginal likelihood of matching revealed labels. Predict the posterior-weighted component means. No evaluation outcomes enter weight updates.
fit: Reuse the training-only center in each leave-one-benchmark-out fold. Independently refit and check it against the previous run. Keep all prior strengths at 2 and random acquisition unchanged.
evaluation: Reuse the five benchmarks, saved item splits, guarded sensitivity, three acquisition seeds and six budgets from the parent protocol. Compute exact finite-pool acquisition expectations for the nonlinear predictor using the complete success-count distribution; verify against exhaustive small fixtures and the old linear formulas.
screening_rule: Advance only if the adaptive candidate improves observed and expected equal-pair and equal-benchmark ALC over Beta(1,1), improves at least four of five benchmark folds in both observed and expected ALC, and preserves the equal-benchmark direction on guarded splits. Additionally compare against the static half-mixture to attribute any benefit to adaptation. Passing is development evidence only.
diagnostics: Report all methods, budgets, seed deltas, and posterior weights; explicitly report the previous BertaQA failure. Outcome-defined group slices are descriptive, never prediction inputs.
constraints: One fixed candidate plus static mixing ablation. No mixture-weight, prior-strength or threshold search; no new downloads, paid services or leaderboard calls.
limitations: This hypothesis was motivated by inspected results; all five datasets remain development data.
At zero labels, there is no evidence to detect a mismatched prior. The initial mixture still transfers information.
Both components are broad priors. More observations need not force either component weight to zero.
Finite-pool expectation removes acquisition noise only, not training uncertainty or benchmark shift.
Existing lexical checks cannot rule out all semantic overlap; model identities may recur across folds.
